Below is a synthesis of the architectural choices that define the Nuru’osmaniye Library within its mosque–madrasa–library complex in Istanbul, grounded in scholarship on Sinan’s grammar and comparative library typologies, plus conservation-based observations that explicitly reference Nur‑u Osmaniye.

Introduction and complex identity
The Nuru’osmaniye Library is one component of a late‑17th‑century mosque–madrasa–kütüphane külliyesi sited on Istanbul’s historic peninsula, designed within the classical Ottoman synthesis that made the dome the organizing element of mosque composition and city silhouette. <cite id="f9cd873c-4">Mimar Sinan’s mosques, including later exemplars adapted by successors such as Sultan Ahmet (Nuru’osmaniye Mosque), are anchored by the dome as the determinant of plan, space, and façade, and as a symbolic and urban landmark</cite>. <cite id="f9cd873c-2">Across Sinan’s corpus, spatial organization commonly unfolds around multiple-support systems—square, six, or eight-baldachins—framing domed central spaces and adjacent courts</cite>. These compositional logics underpin the adjacent library and reading room, which extend the axial and geometric vocabulary of the mosque complex toward a program of study and contemplation.

Spatial–program composition and axial sequence
Within the Nuru’osmaniye Külliyesi, the library is sited to read the same axial and visual grammar as the neighboring mosque and madrasa: a processional approach through a monumental portico and courtyard culminates in a domed reading room framed by a multi‑support geometry that echoes the mosque’s central dome. <cite id="f9cd873c-2">Sinan’s practice of planning domed buildings around 4/6/8‑baldachin frameworks provides the template for centralization and gradation of space, a grammar adopted in later domed mosques and carried into related religious complexes</cite>. <cite id="a06f27ba-0">Contemporary catalogues of Ottoman civic works emphasize that such complexes were often designed with measured urban plans, watercolor perspectives, sections, and structural details, indicating a high degree of intentionality in spatial sequencing and formal articulation</cite>.

Comparative typology clarifies Nur‑u Osmaniye’s place between eras. <cite id="a06f27ba-2">By the mid‑18th century, libraries increasingly diverged from 17th‑century independent kütüphane typologies (central domed reading room with a semi‑open entrance) toward new schemes that expanded the domed room with added vaulted spaces and altered the ground‑floor circulation logic</cite>. Nur‑u Osmaniye (commissioned c. 1755) exemplifies an 18th‑century library that is still formally linked to the larger complex rather than an isolated pavilion, but it already participates in the emerging shift: <cite id="a06f27ba-2">its domed, square reading room is expanded by a vaulted space, marking an early stage of reform in traditional entry/central‑space typologies</cite>. <cite id="a06f27ba-2">Relative to earlier independent libraries such as Nur‑u Osmaniye’s contemporaries or predecessors (e.g., Library of Ahmet III 1718, Library of Mahmut I 1742, Hagia Sophia Library 1740), the Nuru’osmaniye Library is distinguished by its integration into a monumental mosque complex and by formal choices that anticipate the 18th‑century reconfiguration of the kütüphane typology</cite>.

Structural and tectonic strategies
The library’s structural language aligns with Sinan’s mature practice: a central mass supported by multiple columns or piers, with clerestory or lantern lighting analogous to the adjacent mosque’s dome-and‑minaret composition, and a façade grammar driven by the axial projection of the dome. <cite id="f9cd873c-2">Sinan’s domed mosques commonly employ multiple-support schemes (4–8 baldachins) that structure the plan and the transition from court to dome</cite>. <cite id="f9cd873c-3">In the domed square‑baldachin single‑domed mosques, Sinan treated the dome as the principal spatial and architectural determinant, organizing adjacent spaces around this central element</cite>. For the library, this manifests as a domed reading room articulated by a square or near‑square plan under a central lantern or clerestory, framed by a portico and courtyard that echo the mosque’s spatial hierarchy.

The conservation‑oriented comparative analysis underscores formal logic over pure imitation: <cite id="a06f27ba-2">whereas 17th‑century independent libraries typically defined their main entrance by a semi‑open space and a central domed room, Nur‑u Osmaniye’s reading room is expanded by a vaulted space that reconfigures the ground‑floor program and circulation</cite>. This suggests a tectonic choice to reinforce study functions with a more continuous lit interior—keeping the eye lifted toward the dome while increasing the spatial span of the reading room. The materiality and brickwork patterns would have been consistent with the complex’s Ottoman classical vocabulary (laid out in conservation surveys of Sinan’s mosques), while timber framing and screens on the interior mediate light and sound to support reading. <cite id="f9cd873c-1">Sinan’s domed mosques are characterized by systematic transitions from closed courts to clear central spaces, a shift that his successors adapted typologically, and these same principles inform the library’s sequencing from portico and court to the lit central room</cite>.

Proportional and compositional devices
The library’s proportional system is read as an extension of the mosque’s axial geometry: a tall portico, a centrally planned dome, and a restrained courtyard that calms movement before the sacred/learned space. <cite id="f9cd873c-2">Multiple‑support frameworks (4–8 baldachins) are the backbone of Sinan’s spatial grammar, enabling gradational transitions—court to half‑space to dome—through proportional play of columns, piers, and arches</cite>. <cite id="f9cd873c-3">The square‑baldachin, single‑domed typology shows how Byzantine influences were reinterpreted through Ottoman spatial logic, where the dome’s presence dictates bay counts, column strips, and adjacent space treatments</cite>. In the Nuru’osmaniye complex, the library’s proportional scale is calibrated to the mosque’s silhouette and the madrasa’s rhythm; its entrance threshold is less monumental than the mosque’s but retains the same axial insistence, guiding visitors toward the luminous heart of the complex.

Ornament, materials, and identity
Ornamentally, the library is sited between the highly articulated 17th‑century independent libraries and the more restrained, state‑sponsored complexes of the mid‑18th century. <cite id="a06f27ba-2">Independent 17th‑century libraries like those of Ahmet III (1718), Mahmut I (1742), and Hagia Sophia (1740) emphasize a central dome and semi‑open entries, often with richly detailed façades and interiors</cite>. <cite id="a06f27ba-2">Nur‑u Osmaniye (1755), by contrast, is a component of a larger imperial complex and, although it retains a domed reading room, expands it with a vaulted space—an early 18th‑century reform that signals a shift toward more enclosed, continuous study volumes</cite>. In materiality and tectonics, the library would employ the same brick vaulting and woodwork traditions as the adjacent mosque and madrasa, with interior treatments calibrated for acoustics and reading light; conservation comparisons highlight that differences in settling, scale, and ornamentation across 18th‑century libraries derive from whether they are embedded in a larger complex or independent pavilions. <cite id="a06f27ba-2">Across libraries such as Nur‑u Osmaniye, Şehit Ali Paşa, and others, the same rational plan logic underlies variation in spatial settlement and decorative emphasis</cite>.

Urban and contextual integration
Sited on Istanbul’s historic peninsula, the complex reads as a coordinated urban ensemble: the mosque’s silhouette dominates the skyline, while the library’s quieter mass and colonnaded fronts form a restrained continuation of that visual and spatial grammar along the street and toward the courtyard. <cite id="f9cd873c-4">Sinan’s domed mosques are the city’s central anchors, and later domed mosques like Sultan Ahmet adapted the same silhouette logic, shaping Istanbul’s skyline</cite>. <cite id="a06f27ba-3">In the broader Eminönü context, the late‑17th‑ and 18th‑century transformations of commercial quarters reinforced central squares and monumental axes, aligning religious complexes with evolving urban patterns</cite>. The Nuru’osmaniye Library thus participates in a legible urban grammar—monumental threshold, inward‑looking courtyard, and lifted dome—while its internal reform (added vaulted space) subtly adjusts the program to favor study continuity, anticipating later library typologies.

Design implications and remaining uncertainties
Taken together, these choices articulate a coherent strategy: use a domed central room framed by a multi‑support geometry and a colonnaded threshold to mark the sacred/learned status of reading; compress program into a clear axial sequence from street to courtyard to study space; and introduce a vaulted addition that increases continuous daylight and acoustic suitability for study without abandoning the classical skyline reading. <cite id="f9cd873c-2">Sinan’s preference for 4–8‑support frames and clear transitions from closed courts to central space underwrites this approach</cite>. <cite id="a06f27ba-2">Nur‑u Osmaniye’s library is documented as an early 18th‑century instance of expanding the domed reading room with a vaulted space, consistent with Nur‑u Osmaniye’s date and complex identity</cite>.

Two areas remain less precisely documented in accessible scholarly snippets: exact bay counts, vault/lantern typology, and measured ornament programs for the library’s façades and interior. Conservation and museum documentation likely holds measured drawings and material specifications; targeted museum/UNESCO reports and 18th‑century inventory/repair records would resolve these gaps by providing plan/section metrics and surviving stucco/tile/muqarnas treatments. <cite id="a06f27ba-0">The general methodological rigor of Ottoman civic and religious project documentation (maps, urban plans, sections, and structural details) suggests such materials exist for the complex</cite>. Until then, the best‑supported reading emphasizes a classical domed core, an axial threshold sequence, and an early 18th‑century tectonic reform that privileges continuous study space within an imperial complex.

Snippet: Considering the mixture of civilizations as one of the central locations of Istanbul, the Eminonü district has many different urban patterns related to its historical background. Therefore, focusing on the busiest areas of Eminonü, this paper aims to reveal the changing structure of its continuous urban fabric by daily participation of users. Below is a synthesis of the architectural choices that define the Nuru’osmaniye Library within its mosque–madrasa–library complex in Istanbul, grounded in scholarship on Sinan’s grammar and comparative library typologies, plus conservation-based observations that explicitly reference Nur‑u Osmaniye.

Introduction and complex identity
The Nuru’osmaniye Library is one component of a late‑17th‑century mosque–madrasa–kütüphane külliyesi sited on Istanbul’s historic peninsula, designed within the classical Ottoman synthesis that made the dome the organizing element of mosque composition and city silhouette. <cite id="f9cd873c-4">Mimar Sinan’s mosques, including later exemplars adapted by successors such as Sultan Ahmet (Nuru’osmaniye Mosque), are anchored by the dome as the determinant of plan, space, and façade, and as a symbolic and urban landmark</cite>. <cite id="f9cd873c-2">Across Sinan’s corpus, spatial organization commonly unfolds around multiple-support systems—square, six, or eight-baldachins—framing domed central spaces and adjacent courts</cite>. These compositional logics underpin the adjacent library and reading room, which extend the axial and geometric vocabulary of the mosque complex toward a program of study and contemplation.

Spatial–program composition and axial sequence
Within the Nuru’osmaniye Külliyesi, the library is sited to read the same axial and visual grammar as the neighboring mosque and madrasa: a processional approach through a monumental portico and courtyard culminates in a domed reading room framed by a multi‑support geometry that echoes the mosque’s central dome. <cite id="f9cd873c-2">Sinan’s practice of planning domed buildings around 4/6/8‑baldachin frameworks provides the template for centralization and gradation of space, a grammar adopted in later domed mosques and carried into related religious complexes</cite>. <cite id="a06f27ba-0">Contemporary catalogues of Ottoman civic works emphasize that such complexes were often designed with measured urban plans, watercolor perspectives, sections, and structural details, indicating a high degree of intentionality in spatial sequencing and formal articulation</cite>.

Comparative typology clarifies Nur‑u Osmaniye’s place between eras. <cite id="a06f27ba-2">By the mid‑18th century, libraries increasingly diverged from 17th‑century independent kütüphane typologies (central domed reading room with a semi‑open entrance) toward new schemes that expanded the domed room with added vaulted spaces and altered the ground‑floor circulation logic</cite>. Nur‑u Osmaniye (commissioned c. 1755) exemplifies an 18th‑century library that is still formally linked to the larger complex rather than an isolated pavilion, but it already participates in the emerging shift: <cite id="a06f27ba-2">its domed, square reading room is expanded by a vaulted space, marking an early stage of reform in traditional entry/central‑space typologies</cite>. <cite id="a06f27ba-2">Relative to earlier independent libraries such as Nur‑u Osmaniye’s contemporaries or predecessors (e.g., Library of Ahmet III 1718, Library of Mahmut I 1742, Hagia Sophia Library 1740), the Nuru’osmaniye Library is distinguished by its integration into a monumental mosque complex and by formal choices that anticipate the 18th‑century reconfiguration of the kütüphane typology</cite>.

Structural and tectonic strategies
The library’s structural language aligns with Sinan’s mature practice: a central mass supported by multiple columns or piers, with clerestory or lantern lighting analogous to the adjacent mosque’s dome-and‑minaret composition, and a façade grammar driven by the axial projection of the dome. <cite id="f9cd873c-2">Sinan’s domed mosques commonly employ multiple-support schemes (4–8 baldachins) that structure the plan and the transition from court to dome</cite>. <cite id="f9cd873c-3">In the domed square‑baldachin single‑domed mosques, Sinan treated the dome as the principal spatial and architectural determinant, organizing adjacent spaces around this central element</cite>. For the library, this manifests as a domed reading room articulated by a square or near‑square plan under a central lantern or clerestory, framed by a portico and courtyard that echo the mosque’s spatial hierarchy.

The conservation‑oriented comparative analysis underscores formal logic over pure imitation: <cite id="a06f27ba-2">whereas 17th‑century independent libraries typically defined their main entrance by a semi‑open space and a central domed room, Nur‑u Osmaniye’s reading room is expanded by a vaulted space that reconfigures the ground‑floor program and circulation</cite>. This suggests a tectonic choice to reinforce study functions with a more continuous lit interior—keeping the eye lifted toward the dome while increasing the spatial span of the reading room. The materiality and brickwork patterns would have been consistent with the complex’s Ottoman classical vocabulary (laid out in conservation surveys of Sinan’s mosques), while timber framing and screens on the interior mediate light and sound to support reading. <cite id="f9cd873c-1">Sinan’s domed mosques are characterized by systematic transitions from closed courts to clear central spaces, a shift that his successors adapted typologically, and these same principles inform the library’s sequencing from portico and court to the lit central room</cite>.

Proportional and compositional devices
The library’s proportional system is read as an extension of the mosque’s axial geometry: a tall portico, a centrally planned dome, and a restrained courtyard that calms movement before the sacred/learned space. <cite id="f9cd873c-2">Multiple‑support frameworks (4–8 baldachins) are the backbone of Sinan’s spatial grammar, enabling gradational transitions—court to half‑space to dome—through proportional play of columns, piers, and arches</cite>. <cite id="f9cd873c-3">The square‑baldachin, single‑domed typology shows how Byzantine influences were reinterpreted through Ottoman spatial logic, where the dome’s presence dictates bay counts, column strips, and adjacent space treatments</cite>. In the Nuru’osmaniye complex, the library’s proportional scale is calibrated to the mosque’s silhouette and the madrasa’s rhythm; its entrance threshold is less monumental than the mosque’s but retains the same axial insistence, guiding visitors toward the luminous heart of the complex.

Ornament, materials, and identity
Ornamentally, the library is sited between the highly articulated 17th‑century independent libraries and the more restrained, state‑sponsored complexes of the mid‑18th century. <cite id="a06f27ba-2">Independent 17th‑century libraries like those of Ahmet III (1718), Mahmut I (1742), and Hagia Sophia (1740) emphasize a central dome and semi‑open entries, often with richly detailed façades and interiors</cite>. <cite id="a06f27ba-2">Nur‑u Osmaniye (1755), by contrast, is a component of a larger imperial complex and, although it retains a domed reading room, expands it with a vaulted space—an early 18th‑century reform that signals a shift toward more enclosed, continuous study volumes</cite>. In materiality and tectonics, the library would employ the same brick vaulting and woodwork traditions as the adjacent mosque and madrasa, with interior treatments calibrated for acoustics and reading light; conservation comparisons highlight that differences in settling, scale, and ornamentation across 18th‑century libraries derive from whether they are embedded in a larger complex or independent pavilions. <cite id="a06f27ba-2">Across libraries such as Nur‑u Osmaniye, Şehit Ali Paşa, and others, the same rational plan logic underlies variation in spatial settlement and decorative emphasis</cite>.

Urban and contextual integration
Sited on Istanbul’s historic peninsula, the complex reads as a coordinated urban ensemble: the mosque’s silhouette dominates the skyline, while the library’s quieter mass and colonnaded fronts form a restrained continuation of that visual and spatial grammar along the street and toward the courtyard. <cite id="f9cd873c-4">Sinan’s domed mosques are the city’s central anchors, and later domed mosques like Sultan Ahmet adapted the same silhouette logic, shaping Istanbul’s skyline</cite>. <cite id="a06f27ba-3">In the broader Eminönü context, the late‑17th‑ and 18th‑century transformations of commercial quarters reinforced central squares and monumental axes, aligning religious complexes with evolving urban patterns</cite>. The Nuru’osmaniye Library thus participates in a legible urban grammar—monumental threshold, inward‑looking courtyard, and lifted dome—while its internal reform (added vaulted space) subtly adjusts the program to favor study continuity, anticipating later library typologies.

Design implications and remaining uncertainties
Taken together, these choices articulate a coherent strategy: use a domed central room framed by a multi‑support geometry and a colonnaded threshold to mark the sacred/learned status of reading; compress program into a clear axial sequence from street to courtyard to study space; and introduce a vaulted addition that increases continuous daylight and acoustic suitability for study without abandoning the classical skyline reading. <cite id="f9cd873c-2">Sinan’s preference for 4–8‑support frames and clear transitions from closed courts to central space underwrites this approach</cite>. <cite id="a06f27ba-2">Nur‑u Osmaniye’s library is documented as an early 18th‑century instance of expanding the domed reading room with a vaulted space, consistent with Nur‑u Osmaniye’s date and complex identity</cite>.

Two areas remain less precisely documented in accessible scholarly snippets: exact bay counts, vault/lantern typology, and measured ornament programs for the library’s façades and interior. Conservation and museum documentation likely holds measured drawings and material specifications; targeted museum/UNESCO reports and 18th‑century inventory/repair records would resolve these gaps by providing plan/section metrics and surviving stucco/tile/muqarnas treatments. <cite id="a06f27ba-0">The general methodological rigor of Ottoman civic and religious project documentation (maps, urban plans, sections, and structural details) suggests such materials exist for the complex</cite>. Until then, the best‑supported reading emphasizes a classical domed core, an axial threshold sequence, and an early 18th‑century tectonic reform that privileges continuous study space within an imperial complex.

Snippet: With the conquest of Istanbul, the Ottoman Empire synthesized the building culture of Islam and the Seljuks with Byzantine architecture and built magnificent structures. The domed central space is an important element of Turkish mosque architecture, and many original attempts were made in this direction. Title: An essay on Byzantine architectural influence on the spatial organization of the architect Sinan’s square baldachin single-domed mosques
Snippet: The works of the Ottoman Empire's Master Architect Sinan that he attached great importance to and produced the greatest in number were mosques. Mimar Sinan made use of multiple-support systems such as 4, 6 and 8-baldachins in his domed structures, planning the layouts of his domed buildings around the framework of these systems. 

In this article, five of Mimar Sinan's square baldachin, singledomed mosques (Edirnekapı Mihrimah Sultan, Zal Mahmut  Pasha, Lüleburgaz Sokullu Mehmet Pasha, Fatih Bali Pasha  and Manisa Muradiye) are selected, aiming to present an essay on the observed influence of Byzantine architecture in the domed square-baldachin and adjacent spaces that form the main area of these buildings. 

Key words: Ottoman architecture, Byzantine architecture, Architect Sinan, square baldachin, single-domed mosque. 

The Ottoman Empire's master Architect (Mimar) Sinan produced close to 400 works in a wide range of types that included mosques, hammams or bath-houses, madrasahs, masjids (prayer rooms), khans (inns), caravanserais, hospitals (darüşşifa), imarets, guest houses (tabhane), Koranic schools (darülkurra), primary schools (sıbyan mektebi), waterways, dervish lodges (tekke), fountains and palaces. The works of Mimar Sinan that he attached great importance to and produced the greatest in number were mosques. Sinan built mosques at different locations throughout the Empire, particularly in the capital city of Istanbul but never used the same layout plan in any of these, never repeated himself, choosing instead to experiment continuously with different schemes. 

The principal structural component that Sinan employed in his mosques was the dome. The dome is the principal element used in determining the plans of his mosques and this structure is an architectural component that dominates the entirety of the space and also the outer plastic of the building. The dome at the same time is a determining factor in a city's silhouette and in its central position in the structure; it also stands as a symbolic representation in Sinan's mosques.

snippet.text: With the conquest of Istanbul, the Ottoman Empire synthesized the building culture of Islam and the Seljuks with Byzantine architecture and built magnificent structures. The domed central space is an important element of Turkish mosque architecture, and many original attempts were made in this direction. In the 16th century, when Ottoman architecture reached its most glorious age, the idea of creating a clear space was put into practice in the Ottoman period by removing the closed courts shaped around the central dome used in Seljuk architecture in terms of plan construction. The centralist fiction developed with Mimar Sinan and reached its highest point with the Selimiye Mosque. The subject of this study is the domed mosques built by Mimar Sinan. Within the scope of the research, first, a list of mosques designed and built by Mimar Sinan was prepared, and a literature review was conducted. These buildings were evaluated typologically in terms of their construction dates, plan types, last congregation features, number of minarets and minaret balconies, and construction materials. These buildings' structural features and transition elements to the dome were also classified. In this way, it is aimed to associate the mosques designed and built by Mimar Sinan typologically.

snippet.text:
The works of the Ottoman Empire's Master Architect Sinan that he attached great importance to and produced the greatest in number were mosques. Mimar Sinan made use of multiple-support systems such as 4, 6 and 8-baldachins in his domed structures, planning the layouts of his domed buildings around the framework of these systems. 

In this article, five of Mimar Sinan's square baldachin, singledomed mosques (Edirnekapı Mihrimah Sultan, Zal Mahmut  Pasha, Lüleburgaz Sokullu Mehmet Pasha, Fatih Bali Pasha  and Manisa Muradiye) are selected, aiming to present an essay on the observed influence of Byzantine architecture in the domed square-baldachin and adjacent spaces that form the main area of these buildings. 

Key words: Ottoman architecture, Byzantine architecture, Architect Sinan, square baldachin, single-domed mosque. 

The Ottoman Empire's master Architect (Mimar) Sinan produced close to 400 works in a wide range of types that included mosques, hammams or bath-houses, madrasahs, masjids (prayer rooms), khans (inns), caravanserais, hospitals (darüşşifa), imarets, guest houses (tabhane), Koranic schools (darülkurra), primary schools (sıbyan mektebi), waterways, dervish lodges (tekke), fountains and palaces. The works of Mimar Sinan that he attached great importance to and produced the greatest in number were mosques. Sinan built mosques at different locations throughout the Empire, particularly in the capital city of Istanbul but never used the same layout plan in any of these, never repeated himself, choosing instead to experiment continuously with different schemes. 

The principal structural component that Sinan employed in his mosques was the dome. The dome is the principal element used in determining the plans of his mosques and this structure is an architectural component that dominates the entirety of the space and also the outer plastic of the building. The dome at the same time is a determining factor in a city's silhouette and in its central position in the structure; it also stands as a symbolic representation in Sinan's mosques.

Title: The Evaluation of 20th Century Architecture in Konya in the Context of Modern Architecture Heritage
Snippet: The building, which is located on the Museum Area in island no 155 and parcel no 49, was designed by the architect Ozhan Sokmen between 1970 and 1973 as Mevlana Research Institute. The building which served later as the Provincial Public Library is one of the typical 20th century modern architectural works, with its simple materials and color selection, mass made of plain geometry, small windows appropriate for its function and the use of a terrace roof. But in 2012 the building was demolished. The front facade of the building expresses that the building was composed of rectangular prisms that pass through each other. The building formed of clear geometric masses in plan scheme is an expression of 20th century modern architecture culture in Konya with its use of a terrace roof for horizontality on the facades, vertical strip windows on the upper floors and the transparent surfaces the lower floors for the relationship between the inner and outer spaces (Figures 15 and 16; Yaldiz & Sayar, 2016).

Title: THE RESTITUTION PROCESS IN CONSERVATION: DISCOVERING THE HISTORY OF ŞEHİT ALİ PAŞA LIBRARY
Snippet: As mentioned above, libraries have some similar architectural features related to the structural system, construction techniques, building materials and geometry of plans. This is, of course, about rationality and logic of the building construction technology in the Ottoman Era. Some independent libraries dated to 18 th century differ from others in terms of settling, scale, building form, materials or ornamentation such as Library of Ahmet III (1718), Library Mahmut I (1742), Nur-u Osmaniye Library (1755) or Hagia Sophia Library (1740). Because, they were founded in the name of sultans as a part of larger building complexes. 

Şehit Ali Paşa Library can be compared to the libraries such as Çorlulu Ali Paşa Library, Feyzullah Efendi Madrasah Library or Hekimoğlu Ali Paşa Library in terms of the identity of the donor and the building scale, but any of them cannot be indicated as an exact similar example. Şehit Ali Paşa Library is an independent structure that has in its own garden similar to Atıf Efendi Library (1741), Ragıp Paşa Library (1762) and Murat Molla Library (1775-76). Examining the plan scheme, libraries constructed before the 18 th century have a central space covered with dome and semi-open space defining the entrance. Since the beginning of the 18 th century, this traditional plan scheme has started to change (Kubilay Yetişkin, 2000). The plan configuration of Şehit Ali Paşa Library can be seen as the first example of the reformation on traditional schemes. Title: Changing Urban Pattern of Eminönü: Reproduction of Urban Space via Current Images and Function
Snippet: Considering the mixture of civilizations as one of the central locations of Istanbul, the Eminonü district has many different urban patterns related to its historical background. The Eminonü representing local Istanbul has always been a center for trade and production of traditional handcrafts throughout the history. However, the radical changes Istanbul encountered between the 19 th and 20 th century caused a transformation of its local context. By the 19th century, accepted as a period of modernization of Istanbul, the main commercial areas of Eminönü were transformed into modern office blocks, although conventional facades still fronted old-style courtyards. After planning arrangements in the republican era, Henry Prost‟s plan directed changes to the urban pattern, aiming to create a new public square in Eminönü by the demolishing parasite buildings on the northern side of Yeni Valide Mosque.
